lead: Steel and concrete act as one material only because of bond, the shear stress along the surface of each bar that passes force between the bar and the concrete around it. A bar cannot reach its design stress at the point where it starts; the force has to be built up by bond over a length. That length is the development length L<sub>d</sub>, and it decides how far bars must run past a critical section, into a support, round a hook or beyond a cut-off. Most anchorage failures in real buildings are failures to provide it.
prereq: You need: the design stress 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> of steel (design philosophies and partial safety factors) and the moment of resistance of a singly reinforced section (limit state design of beams).

items: Adhesion: the chemical grip of hardened cement paste on the steel. It breaks at a very small slip.
Friction: resistance to sliding once the bar starts to move, helped by shrinkage of the concrete onto the bar.
Mechanical bearing: the ribs of a deformed bar bear on the concrete like small keys. This is the main source of bond for the deformed (TMT) bars used today.

blocks.text: Flexural bond is needed wherever the bar force changes because the moment changes; anchorage bond is needed at a bar end, where the whole force must pass into the concrete. IS 456 does not check local flexural bond stress in the limit state method; it requires L<sub>d</sub> on both sides of every section where a bar is fully stressed, plus the check at supports and points of inflection.

Bond can fail in two ways. In pull-out, the bar slides and shears the concrete between its ribs; this needs good confinement and is the case the bond stresses of IS 456 assume. In splitting, the wedging action of the ribs splits the cover along the bar. Splitting governs when the cover is thin or the bars are crowded, which is why cover, spacing and stirrups matter for bond.

A bar of diameter φ carries the force σ<sub>s</sub> π φ²/4. Over an embedded length L<sub>d</sub> the bond force is τ<sub>bd</sub> π φ L<sub>d</sub>. Setting the two equal and cancelling π φ gives the formula.

blocks.where: L<sub>d</sub> is the development length (mm); φ is the bar diameter (mm); σ<sub>s</sub> is the stress to be developed, 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> at the limit state of collapse (N/mm²); τ<sub>bd</sub> is the design bond stress (N/mm²).

blocks.text: IS 456 gives τ<sub>bd</sub> for plain bars in tension: 1.2 N/mm² for M20, 1.4 for M25, 1.5 for M30, 1.7 for M35 and 1.9 for M40 and above. For deformed bars these values are increased by 60 %, and for bars in compression by a further 25 %. For bundled bars, L<sub>d</sub> of each bar is increased by 10 % for two bars in contact, 20 % for three and 33 % for four. So the M25 value for deformed bars in tension is 1.4 × 1.6 = 2.24 N/mm².

L<sub>d</sub> depends on the bar diameter, the steel stress and the concrete grade only, not on the span or the load. Many designers keep this table at hand and write L<sub>d</sub> as a multiple of φ: a 16 mm Fe415 bar in M25 needs 40.3 × 16 = 645 mm.

items: Deformed bars may be used without hooks if L<sub>d</sub> is available. Plain bars in tension normally get hooks.
Anchorage value of a bend: 4φ for each 45° of bend, up to 16φ. A 90° bend is worth 8φ; a standard U-type hook is worth 16φ. The anchorage value counts as part of L<sub>d</sub>.
In compression, hooks and bends add nothing; only the straight projected length counts.
At a simple support, at least one third of the positive moment steel must run into the support for a length L<sub>d</sub>/3 (one quarter in continuous beams).

blocks.where: Checked at simple supports and points of inflection; it limits the bar diameter. M<sub>1</sub> is the moment of resistance with all bars reaching the section stressed to 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> (N·mm); V is the shear there (N); L<sub>0</sub> is the anchorage beyond the centre of the support plus the anchorage value of any hook (mm), or at a point of inflection the greater of d and 12φ. Use 1.3 when a compressive reaction confines the bar ends, otherwise 1.0.

blocks.text: Near a support the shear is large, so the bar force climbs quickly from zero; M<sub>1</sub>/V is roughly the distance over which the moment reaches M<sub>1</sub>. A bar too thick for that distance pulls out before reaching its full force. The cure is smaller bars, or a bend or hook to increase L<sub>0</sub>.

examples.question: Find the development length of a 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete (a) in tension and (b) in compression. Also find the bond force such a bar must pass to the concrete.
steps: Bond stress in tension: τ<sub>bd</sub> = 1.4 × 1.6 = 2.24 N/mm² (plain-bar value for M25 raised by 60 % for deformed bars).
Compression: τ<sub>bd</sub> = 2.24 × 1.25 = 2.80 N/mm², so L<sub>d</sub> = 5776.8/(4 × 2.80) = 515.8 mm, say 520 mm.
Bar force: 361.05 × π × 16²/4 = 361.05 × 201.1 = 72,590 N = 72.6 kN. Check: 2.24 × π × 16 × 644.7 = 72,590 N, the same force passed by bond over L<sub>d</sub>.
examples.answer: L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm in tension and 520 mm in compression (515.8 mm computed); the bar force to be developed is 72.6 kN.
examples.check:
import math
fs=0.87*415
Lt=16*fs/(4*2.24)
Lc=16*fs/(4*2.8)
F=fs*math.pi*16**2/4
print(round(Lt,1),round(Lc,1),round(F/1e3,1),round(2.24*math.pi*16*Lt/1e3,1))

examples.question: At the simple support of the beam b = 300 mm, d = 550 mm (M25, Fe415), two 20 mm bottom bars continue into a 300 mm wide masonry support; the end cover is 30 mm. The shear at the support is V = 180 kN and the reaction compresses the bar ends. Check the anchorage.
steps: Area at the support: A<sub>st</sub> = 2 × 314.2 = 628.3 mm². Neutral axis: x<sub>u</sub> = 0.87 × 415 × 628.3/(0.36 × 25 × 300) = 84.0 mm.

L<sub>0</sub>, straight bar beyond the support centre: 300/2 − 30 = 120 mm. So 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> = 843.9 + 120 = 963.9 mm ≥ L<sub>d</sub> = 805.9 mm. The diameter is acceptable without a hook.

Embedment into the support: L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 268.6 mm; the bars have 300 − 30 = 270 mm from the face to their ends, just enough. Both bars, half of the four bars at midspan, reach the support, more than the one third required.
examples.answer: L<sub>d</sub> = 805.9 mm ≤ 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub> = 963.9 mm, and the 270 mm embedment exceeds L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 268.6 mm, so two straight 20 mm bars are adequately anchored.

traps: Using the plain-bar bond stress for deformed bars. For M25 deformed bars in tension τ<sub>bd</sub> = 2.24 N/mm², not 1.4 N/mm²; using 1.4 makes L<sub>d</sub> 1.6 times too long (1032 mm instead of 645 mm for a 16 mm bar).
Using f<sub>y</sub> instead of 0.87 f<sub>y</sub> for σ<sub>s</sub> in tension.
Counting a hook towards L<sub>d</sub> of a bar in compression. Only the straight projected length counts in compression.
Treating the support width as the available anchorage. The simple-support check is L<sub>d</sub> ≤ 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V + L<sub>0</sub>, with L<sub>0</sub> measured beyond the centre of the support.
Forgetting to increase L<sub>d</sub> for bundled bars (10, 20 or 33 % for two, three or four bars).

quiz.a: The length a bar must be embedded in concrete, on each side of a section where it carries its design force, so that bond can build up that force: L<sub>d</sub> = φ σ<sub>s</sub>/(4 τ<sub>bd</sub>).

quiz.q: What is τ<sub>bd</sub> for M25 concrete and deformed bars in tension and in compression?
Why do deformed bars need a shorter development length than plain bars?
quiz.a: Their ribs bear on the concrete, so the design bond stress is 60 % higher. L<sub>d</sub> is inversely proportional to τ<sub>bd</sub>, so L<sub>d</sub> is shorter by the same factor.

quiz.q: Find L<sub>d</sub> for a 20 mm Fe500 deformed bar in M30 concrete in tension.
What anchorage value does a 90° bend give a 16 mm bar, and how much straight length is then needed to make up L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm?
quiz.a: 8φ = 8 × 16 = 128 mm. Straight length needed = 645 − 128 = 517 mm (measured to the start of the bend).

quiz.q: In worked example 2, the bars were changed to 25 mm. Would the support check still pass?
quiz.a: L<sub>d</sub> = 25 × 361.05/8.96 = 1007.4 mm. With 2 bars of 25 mm (981.7 mm²), x<sub>u</sub> = 131.3 mm and M<sub>1</sub> = 175.6 kN·m, so 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V = 1268.2 mm and 1268.2 + 120 = 1388.2 mm ≥ 1007.4 mm: it passes. But L<sub>d</sub>/3 = 335.8 mm is more than the 270 mm available, so the bars need a 90° bend at the end.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer codes such as Eurocode 2 and ACI 318 make the bond strength depend on cover, bar spacing and confining steel, so a well-confined bar gets a shorter anchorage. Headed bars, with a forged plate at the end, anchor in a fraction of L<sub>d</sub> and are used in crowded beam-column joints. Glass-fibre (GFRP) bars bond differently from steel and have their own rules. Search for 'headed reinforcement', 'bond-slip relationship' and 'GFRP bar development length'.

figure.caption: The two 20 mm bars at the simple support of worked example 2. L<sub>d</sub> = 806 mm fits within L<sub>0</sub> + 1.3 M<sub>1</sub>/V = 964 mm, and the 270 mm inside the support exceeds L<sub>d</sub>/3.
